newsitem.title: INDIA: Gold - Indian sub-continent prices seen subdued.
newsitem.headline: Gold - Indian sub-continent prices seen subdued.

text.p: Enough supplies of imported gold in India and poor demand in Pakistan may keep prices down in the sub-continent during the next few days, dealers said on Monday.
They said Indian demand, coming mainly from wedding season buying, could match increased arrivals of imported metal may cushion the downward pressures.
"A weak global trend and relatively firm local prices have triggered higher imports of gold by Indian expatriates, said Bhayabhai Sanghvi, a leading dealer.
In the week to Monday standard gold fell 30 rupees per 10 grammes to 4,750 rupees on the Bombay bullion market as supplies of imported gold outmatched demand.

Dealers estimate the cost of imported gold at around 4,720 rupees per 10 grammes, which left a margin of 30 rupees. On 10 kgs of gold that Indian expatriates are allowed to bring in once every six months, the margin works out to 30,000 rupees.
"Profit margins are attractive enough to import gold at present," Sanghavi said.
"Going by the weak world trend, any price rise in the local market will be short-lived," Sanghavi said. "The market is more or less likely to remain subdued to steady in the coming days."
Dealers in Pakistan's commercial city of Karachi said gold prices are likely to remain mixed in the current week because of subdued demand.
Inflation had curtailed savings and eroded the people's purchasing power, said dealer Farooq Qureshi at the Karachi Saraffa (bullion) market.
In Dubai, traders and wholesalers on Sunday reported strong demand for the metal from India, which helped compensate for a downturn in the Gulf Arab emirate's own retail market.
Dubai is a key distribution hub for India, a leading gold consuming nation.
"Indian demand is very strong. It is wedding season now and prices are low...It will probably stay like this until the beginning of the monsoon in June," said a Dubai trader.
Alhough Indian sub-continent bullion demand traditionally tails off during monsoons from June to September, traders said prices at current levels continued to fan demand there.
Buoyant Indian demand is expected to push Dubai's bullion imports to over 400 tonnes this year from 350 tonnes in 1996, according to analysts.
